title: Adding: the resultant and the equilibrant

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the needle on the ring drop to zero when you tap "equilibrant" and its dashed arrow closes the nose-to-tail chain.
interactive.title: Forces on a ring
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A small ring sits on the left. Two ropes pull on it, and later three. Each rope's pull is an arrow from the ring. You can drag an arrow's nose to change that pull. Beside the ring, the same arrows are laid nose to tail. The second starts where the first ends. The resultant runs from the first tail to the last nose. It is the gap the chain leaves. A needle on the ring points along the net pull. Its length and a readout give its size. A button adds the equilibrant. This is a dashed arrow from the last nose back to the first tail. It is the resultant turned round. So the chain closes and the needle drops to zero. In a puzzle, a wrong pick is drawn in red, so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The ring is treated as a single point. So every pull acts at the same place. On a larger body, pulls can act at different points. Then they can also turn it. That turning effect is called a moment. It needs another kind of product, the cross product, in lesson 6. Three pulls in balance that are not parallel must also meet at one point. Lesson 6 shows why. The ropes are drawn straight and weightless. Everything here lies flat on the page. Pulls in 3-D add the same way, with their k parts added too. The puzzles use example values, rounded to two decimal places.

explain.text:
Vectors add nose to tail. Draw the second arrow from where the first one ends. The sum runs from the first tail to the last nose. It is called the [[resultant]].[^1] The resultant is the gap the chain leaves, not the chain's length. So you cannot add vectors by adding their sizes.[^2] Take two 3 kN pulls on a ring. If they point the same way, the chain is one straight line. Then they make 6 kN. At 90° apart, the chain bends. The gap shrinks to √(3² + 3²) = 4.24 kN. At 120° apart, the second arrow turns 120° off the first one's line. So the chain's corner is 180° − 120° = 60°. Two 3 kN sides with 60° between them make a triangle with three equal sides. So the gap is 3 kN. If they pull opposite ways, the second arrow comes straight back. Then the gap is nothing. Sizes add only when the pulls point the same way.

A drawing shows the answer. The parts give it exactly. Each arrow is its across part and its up part, laid nose to tail. So a chain of arrows is a chain of across parts and up parts. Their order does not change where the chain ends. So you can gather all the across parts together. They lie on one line, so they add as plain numbers. The up parts add the same way.[^3] Take pull A, 4i + 1j kN, and pull B, 1i + 3j kN. Across, 4 + 1 = 5. Up, 1 + 3 = 4. The resultant is 5i + 4j. Pythagoras gives its size: √(5² + 4²) = 6.40 kN. The sizes alone would add to 7.29 kN. Now draw B first and A second. You reach the same nose, because the parts add to the same sums in either order. Each arrow is drawn twice, on opposite sides. So the two chains make a parallelogram. The resultant is its diagonal from the shared tail.

Any gap left in the chain is a net pull. A net pull sets the ring moving. To hold the ring still, the pulls must add to nothing. So it needs one more pull that cancels the resultant. That pull is the [[equilibrant]]. It has the same size as the resultant and points the opposite way.[^4] For A and B it is −5i − 4j, also 6.40 kN. Add it to the chain, and the last nose lands back on the first tail. The gap is gone, so the net pull is zero. Three pulls in balance close into a triangle. This is the [[triangle of forces]]. More pulls close into a polygon. Opposite ropes cancel only along their own line. Take 5 kN east, 5 kN west and 2 kN north. East and west cancel, so 2 kN north is left.

**Vectors add nose to tail, or part by part, to give the resultant. The equilibrant is the equal and opposite pull that closes the chain.**[^4]

analogy.text: Think of a ring final circuit. The cable leaves the consumer unit and runs round the rooms. Then it comes back to the same terminals. Lay its legs nose to tail, and the chain closes, however long it is. The chain ends where it began. So its legs add to nothing, just as balanced pulls do. Now stop the run halfway. The straight line from the board to where you stopped is the gap. It is shorter than the cable you used.
analogy.breaks: A cable's legs are laid one after another along a real route. Pulls on a ring all act at once on one point. The nose-to-tail chain is only a drawing that adds them. Its length means nothing.

practice.text:
- Draw every pull as an arrow from the point it acts on.
- Resolve each one into i and j parts. Give each part its sign.
- Add all the i parts. Then add all the j parts. That pair is the resultant.
- Find its size by Pythagoras on those two sums. Find its angle by the tangent, then check the quarter from the signs.
- Sketch the chain nose to tail. The gap should point the way your parts say.
- For the equilibrant, flip both signs. It has the same size and points the opposite way.

**Rule of thumb:** Sizes add only when the pulls point the same way. Otherwise the resultant is shorter than the sizes added.

**Worked example:** Say three lines pull on a ring: 2i + 1j, 3i − 4j and −1i + 6j kN. Across, 2 + 3 − 1 = 4. Up, 1 − 4 + 6 = 3. The resultant is 4i + 3j. Its size is √(4² + 3²) = 5 kN. Its angle is tan⁻¹(3 ÷ 4) = 36.87° above the x-axis. Both parts are plus, so that is the right quarter. The equilibrant is −4i − 3j, which is 5 kN at 216.87°. The three sizes are 2.24, 5 and 6.08 kN. Added, they would make 13.32 kN.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding the sizes. Two 3 kN pulls at 120° make 3 kN, not 6 kN.
- Using Pythagoras on arrows that are not at right angles. For the 120° pulls it gives 4.24 kN. That is the answer for 90°.
- Thinking opposite ropes cancel everything. They cancel only along their own line.
- Joining the noses of two arrows drawn from one point. That line is not the sum. The sum is the diagonal from their shared tail.
- Drawing the gap backwards, from the last nose to the first tail. That arrow is the equilibrant.
- Flipping only one sign for the equilibrant.
- Working the parts but never drawing the chain. A sketch catches a sign slip.

sources.title: 16.1: Vectors - Engineering LibreTexts
sources.quote: In contrast with scalar quantities, we cannot add, subtract, multiply or divide them by simply adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing the magnitudes.
